title: JavaScript Memory Management Core Check
description: Check your understanding of JavaScript memory lifecycle, stack and heap, references, reachability, garbage collection, memory leaks, weak collections, and cleanup patterns.
author: DailyCoder

questions.prompt: What are the three broad stages of the JavaScript memory lifecycle?
questions.explanation: JavaScript values are allocated, used, and later released when they are no longer reachable.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a value to be reachable?

options.text: The engine can get to it from active roots by following references
It is stored only as a string
It has already been garbage collected

questions.explanation: Reachability means a value can be accessed from roots such as globals, active stack frames, timers, or DOM references.

questions.prompt: Which values usually live on the heap in the stack/heap mental model?

options.text: Only values that are already deleted

questions.explanation: Objects, arrays, and functions are reference values commonly described as living on the heap.

questions.prompt: What commonly causes a stack overflow?

options.text: Recursive calls that never reach a base case

questions.explanation: Unbounded recursion keeps adding call frames until the call stack runs out of space.

options.text: A garbage collection strategy that marks reachable values and sweeps away unreachable ones
A way to sort arrays alphabetically
A syntax rule for class fields

questions.explanation: Mark-and-sweep collection starts at roots, marks reachable values, and reclaims values not marked.

questions.prompt: Do circular references always cause memory leaks in modern JavaScript engines?

options.text: No, cycles can be collected if nothing reachable points to them

questions.explanation: Modern JavaScript garbage collection is reachability-based, so unreachable cycles can be collected.

questions.prompt: Which collection strongly references object keys and can keep them alive?
questions.explanation: A regular `Map` strongly references its keys and values until entries are removed or the map itself is collected.

questions.prompt: What can be used to store metadata for object keys without preventing those keys from being garbage collected?
questions.explanation: `WeakMap` holds object keys weakly, making it useful for metadata tied to object lifetimes.

options.text: They are not iterable and do not expose a reliable size
They replace every need for cleanup

questions.explanation: Weak collections are intentionally not iterable because their entries depend on garbage collection.

questions.prompt: Why can closures affect memory usage?

options.text: A closure can keep variables from its outer scope reachable
A closure deletes all outer variables immediately
A closure can only store primitive values
A closure disables garbage collection globally

questions.explanation: Functions retain the outer variables they use, which can keep large objects or DOM nodes alive.

questions.prompt: Which cleanup is usually needed for a repeating timer?

options.text: Set the callback name to uppercase

questions.explanation: A repeating timer remains active until it is cleared with `clearInterval()`.

questions.prompt: What is the safest rule for `FinalizationRegistry`?

options.text: Do not rely on it for required cleanup because timing is unpredictable
Use it to save important user data
Use it instead of removing event listeners
Expect it to run immediately after `null` assignment

questions.explanation: Finalizers may run late or not before shutdown, so required cleanup should be explicit.
